B1:
Touched fires many times: once per body part (feet, legs, torso) and repeatedly as contacts begin and end within the same frames. The handler runs several times before Destroy takes effect. Also, Destroy runs after the first grant, but further events already queued (with deferred signals) still run. Fix: add a debounce flag (or an attribute) set before granting, and disconnect.
```lua
local part = script.Parent
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local taken = false
local conn
conn = part.Touched:Connect(function(hit)
    if taken then return end
    local plr = Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(hit.Parent)
    if not plr then return end
    local h = hit.Parent:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
    if not h or h.Health <= 0 then return end
    taken = true
    conn:Disconnect()
    plr.leaderstats.Coins.Value += 10
    part:Destroy()
end)
```
For respawning coins, use a per-player debounce table instead, and grant through server-side data.
B2: With StreamingEnabled the client only has the instances near the player. Distant parts (the Door) haven't streamed in yet when the LocalScript runs, so indexing .Door errors. It also means the door can stream out and back in as a new instance, breaking any connection you held. Fix 1: wait for it and handle streaming, for example local door = workspace.Map.Buildings.Hotel:WaitForChild("Door") (better with a timeout, and with each ancestor also waited for). Reconnect if it's removed and re-added via ChildAdded or AncestryChanged. Fix 2 (preferred): tag doors with CollectionService ("Door") and use CollectionService:GetInstanceAddedSignal("Door") plus GetTagged, so each door is hooked whenever it streams in, and clean up on GetInstanceRemovedSignal. Alternatively, set the door model's ModelStreamingMode = Atomic/Persistent (Persistent keeps it always on the client, so use it sparingly), or handle the Touched logic on the server, which always has everything.
B3: Bugs: (1) If the player has left, plr is nil, and plr.UserId errors inside the pcall, but it still returns PurchaseGranted, so they're charged with nothing given. (2) The pcall result is ignored: the DataStore call fails, yet the purchase is granted. Charged, nothing given. (3) Not idempotent, with no PurchaseId record. If the callback runs again (retry, timeout, server crash after the write but before the return), coins are added twice. (4) GetAsync followed by SetAsync isn't atomic, so concurrent writes or race conditions lose or duplicate data. Two requests instead of one UpdateAsync. (5) The DataStore key should use info.PlayerId (works even when the player is offline), not plr. (6) It doesn't check info.ProductId, and it doesn't update the live session data/leaderstats. Corrected: in a single UpdateAsync on key info.PlayerId, if the receipts list contains info.PurchaseId, return it unchanged. Otherwise add 100 coins and record the PurchaseId (keep the last N). If the pcall succeeded, return PurchaseGranted. Otherwise return NotProcessedYet so Roblox retries. If the player is in-game with session-locked data, grant to the session profile and save, and return NotProcessedYet if they aren't loaded.
B4: Remotes serialize arguments. Metatables aren't sent: a table arrives as a plain copy of its data fields (Name, Ammo), so the client copy has no __index and w:Fire() is nil. Functions can't be sent either. Instances are sent as references, and the client only receives them if the instance is replicated to that client. ServerStorage is never replicated, so Muzzle arrives as nil. Fix: send plain data (for example {Name="Rifle", Ammo=30} or just an id) and rebuild the object on the client with a shared ModuleScript in ReplicatedStorage: local w = setmetatable(data, Weapon) or Weapon.new(data). Put assets the client needs in ReplicatedStorage (or clone them into workspace), or send an asset name the client looks up. Also avoid mixed or sparse tables and non-string keys in remote payloads.
B5:
workspace:Raycast(origin, direction) uses the length of the direction vector as the ray's distance. .Unit gives length 1, so the ray only travels 1 stud. It also starts inside the shooter's own character, which it may hit. Fix: give the direction a real length and exclude the shooter.
```lua
local params = RaycastParams.new()
params.FilterType = Enum.RaycastFilterType.Exclude
params.FilterDescendantsInstances = {shooterCharacter}
local dir = (target - origin).Unit * 300 -- max range
local r = workspace:Raycast(origin, dir, params)
if r then print(r.Instance, r.Position) end
```
(Or use (target - origin) directly to reach exactly the target, clamped to max range.) Do hit validation on the server.
B6: When the last player leaves, the server starts shutting down. PlayerRemoving may fire, but the server can close before the async SetAsync completes. During shutdown (or a server crash), PlayerRemoving might not finish at all, so the save is cut off. Fix: use game:BindToClose to save every remaining player before shutdown (it gives up to about 30 s). Save in parallel (task.spawn per player), and wait for those saves, plus any PlayerRemoving saves already in flight, to finish within a deadline of about 25 s. Track in-flight saves so BindToClose waits for them, and don't double-save. Use UpdateAsync with retries, plus periodic autosave (every 60-120 s with jitter) so a crash loses little. Skip BindToClose saving in Studio if it's not needed (RunService:IsStudio()), or keep it short. ProfileStore and session-lock libraries handle this.
B7:
```lua
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local UseAbility = game.ReplicatedStorage.Remotes.UseAbility
local COOLDOWN = 2
local lastUse: {[Player]: number} = {}

UseAbility.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, abilityId)
    if typeof(abilityId) ~= "string" then return end
    local now = os.clock()
    local t = lastUse[player]
    if t and now - t < COOLDOWN then return end -- silently drop spam
    local char = player.Character
    local hum = char and char:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
    if not hum or hum.Health <= 0 then return end
    lastUse[player] = now
    performAbility(player, abilityId) -- server-authoritative effect
end)

Players.PlayerRemoving:Connect(function(player)
    lastUse[player] = nil -- no leak
end)
```
The cooldown is enforced on the server with server time. The client cooldown is only cosmetic. Invalid calls are ignored without replying, and the entry is removed when the player leaves (or use a weak-keyed table).

```lua
local MPS = game:GetService("MarketplaceService")
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local DSS = game:GetService("DataStoreService")
local store = DSS:GetDataStore("PlayerData")
local GEMS100 = 123456

local handlers = {
    [GEMS100] = function(data) data.Gems = (data.Gems or 0) + 100 end,
}

MPS.ProcessReceipt = function(info)
    local grant = handlers[info.ProductId]
    if not grant then return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.NotProcessedYet end
    local ok, err = pcall(function()
        store:UpdateAsync("u_" .. info.PlayerId, function(data)
            data = data or { Gems = 0, receipts = {} }
            data.receipts = data.receipts or {}
            if data.receipts[info.PurchaseId] then return data end -- already granted
            grant(data)
            data.receipts[info.PurchaseId] = os.time()
            -- (optionally prune old receipts to keep size bounded)
            return data
        end)
    end)
    if not ok then
        warn("Receipt failed:", err)
        return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.NotProcessedYet -- Roblox retries
    end
    local plr = Players:GetPlayerByUserId(info.PlayerId)
    if plr then -- refresh live state if online
        local ls = plr:FindFirstChild("leaderstats")
        if ls and ls:FindFirstChild("Gems") then ls.Gems.Value += 100 end
    end
    return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.PurchaseGranted
end
```
It works even if the player has left (it keys on PlayerId), and returns Granted only after the save. If you use session-locked profiles, grant to the loaded profile instead, and return NotProcessedYet if the player isn't loaded.

```lua
local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")
local info = TweenInfo.new(0.4, Enum.EasingStyle.Quad, Enum.EasingDirection.Out)
local OPEN = UDim2.new(0.5, 0, 0.5, 0)

    current:Play()

local function close()
    if current then current:Cancel() end
    local t = TweenService:Create(menu, info, {Position = CLOSED})
    current = t
    t.Completed:Connect(function(state)

        end
    end)
    t:Play()
end
```
Visible is only cleared when the slide-out actually completes, not if it's cancelled by reopening.
B10:
```lua
local MAX_RANGE, DAMAGE = 200, 20

local function shoot(player: Player, targetPos: Vector3)
    if typeof(targetPos) ~= "Vector3" or targetPos ~= targetPos then return end
    local char = player.Character
    local head = char and char:FindFirstChild("Head")
    local myHum = char and char:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
    if not head or not myHum or myHum.Health <= 0 then return end

    local origin = head.Position
    local offset = targetPos - origin
    if offset.Magnitude < 1e-3 then return end
    local dir = offset.Unit * MAX_RANGE

    local params = RaycastParams.new()
    params.FilterType = Enum.RaycastFilterType.Exclude
    params.FilterDescendantsInstances = {char}

    local result = workspace:Raycast(origin, dir, params)
    if not result then return end
    local model = result.Instance:FindFirstAncestorOfClass("Model")
    local hum = model and model:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
    if hum and hum.Health > 0 then
        hum:TakeDamage(DAMAGE)
    end
end
```
Also add a server fire-rate check. Accessories/hats may be the hit part, and FindFirstAncestorOfClass("Model") handles that.

```lua
local CollectionService = game:GetService("CollectionService")
local TAG = "KillBrick"
local conns: {[Instance]: RBXScriptConnection} = {}

local function onAdded(part)
    if not part:IsA("BasePart") or conns[part] then return end
    conns[part] = part.Touched:Connect(function(hit)
        local hum = hit.Parent and hit.Parent:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
        if hum and hum.Health > 0 then
            hum.Health = 0
        end
    end)
end

local function onRemoved(part)
    local c = conns[part]
    if c then c:Disconnect(); conns[part] = nil end
end

CollectionService:GetInstanceAddedSignal(TAG):Connect(onAdded)
CollectionService:GetInstanceRemovedSignal(TAG):Connect(onRemoved)
for _, p in CollectionService:GetTagged(TAG) do onAdded(p) end
```
The removed signal also fires when a tagged part is destroyed, so connections never leak. Connect the signals before iterating GetTagged so you don't miss parts.

B13: (a) Buying: the client fires a RemoteEvent (BuyItem with the itemId only), or invokes a RemoteFunction (client to server) if it needs an immediate yes/no result. The server owns the coin balance and the price list, validates everything (types, item exists, affordable, rate limit), deducts and grants atomically in server data, and saves. The client never sends a price or balance. (b) Updating the UI: the server pushes the new balance to the client. The simplest way is a replicated value (leaderstats IntValue or a player attribute) that the UI listens to with .Changed or GetAttributeChangedSignal. Otherwise use a server-to-client RemoteEvent (FireClient). Why not RemoteFunction:InvokeClient: the server would yield waiting on the client. An exploiter can never return, which hangs the server thread forever, or error, or return garbage. If the client leaves, it errors. And you don't need a reply to a UI update anyway. Use fire-and-forget events or replicated state.
B14: Teleport data (TeleportOptions:SetTeleportData, read with Player:GetJoinData().TeleportData) is sent through the client, so it can be tampered with or forged. It's not secure and is size-limited, so use it only for non-authoritative hints (chosen map, party id, cosmetic loadout preferences that the server re-validates). DataStores are server-only and authoritative, so the coin balance must live there. The cost: write and propagation latency plus budgets. Save with UpdateAsync (release a session lock) before teleporting, and load in the destination with session locking. MemoryStores (HashMap/SortedMap/Queue) are fast, server-only, cross-server and expiring. They're good for short-lived handoff state like the match loadout, reservation tokens or party/match assignments, but they aren't durable. Choice: coins live in a DataStore (session-locked, saved before the teleport). The loadout either goes in the DataStore profile or is handed off via a MemoryStore HashMap keyed by userId with a short TTL. Send only a non-sensitive match/reservation id in teleport data, and the server validates everything against the server stores.
B15: Per-instance Scripts (610 copies): each one is a separate script context with its own memory and setup cost, and bug fixes have to be copy-pasted, so versions drift. They're hard to tune, slow to load, and bad with streaming and with instances spawned at runtime (the copies have to be cloned along with them). Tag-driven: tag the instances (Door, Pickup, Turret) with CollectionService, and write one server Script or ModuleScript per behaviour (a system) that handles every tagged instance. Recommended structure: ServerScriptService/Systems/DoorSystem etc., each with a shared module of configuration, using attributes for per-instance settings (speed, reward, range). Each system calls GetTagged plus GetInstanceAddedSignal to set up and GetInstanceRemovedSignal to clean up (disconnect, drop table entries), so instances spawned later, or streamed in on the client, are hooked automatically, and destroyed ones are cleaned. Turrets can be updated in one central Heartbeat loop with throttling instead of 60 separate loops. Client visuals use the same pattern in a LocalScript, which also handles StreamingEnabled stream-in and stream-out.
B16: Give network ownership of the car to the driver: in the VehicleSeat's Occupant change, call SetNetworkOwner(driverPlayer) on the chassis assembly. Return it to the server (SetNetworkOwner(nil)) or set auto ownership when they exit. That gives responsive, lag-free driving, while server ownership would feel laggy. The risk: the owning client fully controls that assembly's physics, so an exploiter can teleport it, speed-hack, fly, fling other players, or skip checkpoints, and the server just accepts the replicated positions. The server must still validate: speed and acceleration plausibility (distance per time against the car's max speed), teleport jumps, position bounds or noclip through walls, and checkpoint order with timing (sequential gates, minimum lap time). Lap counts, finish and race results, and rewards are decided on the server, never reported by the client. Collisions or damage to others should be sanity-checked. On violation, reset the car or take ownership back. Also make sure only the seated driver owns it, and clear ownership on exit or death.
B17: Use UnreliableRemoteEvent (FireServer and FireAllClients are unordered and lossy, with no queuing or resend). It suits high-frequency, replaceable state like aim and position, and it reduces queue pressure. Constraints: packets can be dropped or arrive out of order, and payloads are size-limited (about 1 KB per call, oversized ones are dropped). Handling: send the latest full state each time rather than deltas, include a sequence number or timestamp, and discard stale or out-of-order packets on the receiver. Interpolate or extrapolate on observers. Reduce the rate (10-20 Hz) and only send on meaningful change. Compress: quantize the angles (for example, yaw and pitch as int16 in a buffer), and send Vector3s or buffers instead of tables. Keep important one-time events (fire, hit, reload) on a reliable RemoteEvent. Validate on the server and rate-limit. Character position is already replicated by physics, so you usually only need to send aim.
B18: Split the NPCs into Actors: put each group of NPCs (for example 10-25 per Actor) under an Actor instance with its own Script, or move the NPC scripts under Actors. In each, connect RunService.Heartbeat:ConnectParallel (or call task.desynchronize()) to run the read-only work in parallel: raycasts (workspace:Raycast is parallel-safe), distance and path scoring, target selection. Then call task.synchronize() to apply the results in serial: set Humanoid:MoveTo, CFrames and properties, fire events. Limitations: in the parallel phase you can only read the DataModel. Writes to most properties, creating or destroying instances, and many yielding APIs (PathfindingService:ComputeAsync etc.) are disallowed. Do the writes after synchronize. Actors don't share Lua state: communicate via Actor:SendMessage/BindToMessage, attributes, or SharedTable. Each Actor has its own VM, so module requires are duplicated and there's memory overhead. Per-thread overhead means too many tiny actors is slow. Also throttle the work: stagger NPCs over frames, use lower tick rates for distant NPCs, and cache paths. Profile with the MicroProfiler.
B19: Turn on Workspace.StreamingEnabled. Sensible settings: StreamingMinRadius about 64-128 studs, StreamingTargetRadius about 256-1024 (the default is 64 min / 1024 target; lower it for mobile or dense maps). StreamOutBehavior = Opportunistic (to free memory on low-end devices), StreamingIntegrityMode = MinimumRadiusPause (or PauseOutsideLoadedArea) so players don't fall into unloaded areas. Use Model.ModelStreamingMode: Atomic for models that must arrive whole, Persistent only for a few always-needed models (spawn, key landmarks), PersistentPerPlayer where needed. Set Model.LevelOfDetail = StreamingMesh for distant silhouettes. Use Player:RequestStreamAroundAsync before teleports or cutscenes. Scripts: client code can't assume parts exist. Replace direct indexing with WaitForChild (with timeouts), use CollectionService tag signals or ChildAdded to hook objects as they stream in, and clean up when they stream out (instances may be destroyed and re-created). Keep authoritative logic on the server, which has everything. Don't hold references to far-away parts, and avoid giant single models.
B20: Cause: 80 players x every 5 s = 960 writes/min, far above the write budget (about 300 + 20 x CCU per experience, 60 + 10 x players per server historically), and above the per-key limit (writes to the same key roughly once every 6 s). The requests pile up in the 30-slot request queue, then the queue fills and requests fail, and saves are dropped. SetAsync also blindly overwrites, so a failed or out-of-order write can lose data. Better design: keep data in memory (a session cache or profile) and mark it dirty on change. Autosave each player every 60-120 s, staggered with a random per-player offset and jitter, and only if dirty. Save immediately on important events (purchases, trades), debounced. Save on PlayerRemoving and in BindToClose (parallel, with a deadline). Use UpdateAsync with session locking, pcall plus exponential-backoff retries, and check GetRequestBudgetForRequestType before saving. Keep one key per player (combine stats into one table). Use ProfileStore or a similar library. Put leaderboards and ephemeral counters in MemoryStore or OrderedDataStore at low frequency.
B21: In Studio, open the Assistant panel, then its ... menu > Manage MCP Servers, and toggle "Enable Studio as MCP server" (a green indicator shows it's running). Then point the external client (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI) at it. It replaces the older community/Rust MCP server, which was archived in April 2026. Tools it exposes include: list_roblox_studios (pick the session), get_studio_state, search_game_tree, inspect_instance, script_read, script_search, script_grep, multi_edit (edit scripts), execute_luau, start_stop_play, get_console_output, screen_capture, user_keyboard_input, user_mouse_input, character_navigation, search_asset, insert_asset, upload_image, generate_mesh, generate_material, wait_job_finished and http_get.
B22: Three core instances: InputContext (a group of actions that can be enabled or disabled, with Priority and Sink), InputAction (a semantic action like "Jump" or "Sprint", with a Type: Bool, Direction1D/2D/3D, ViewportPosition) and InputBinding (maps a physical input to the action: KeyCode, gamepad buttons, axes, or UIButton for touch). Bindings are children of actions, and actions are children of contexts. Signals: Bool actions fire InputAction.Pressed and Released, and every type fires StateChanged(newState). You can poll InputAction:GetState() each frame for analog values. Precedence: give the menu's InputContext a higher Priority than the default player-scripts/gameplay context, and set Sink = true so the inputs it binds are consumed and not passed to lower-priority contexts. Enable it when the menu opens (ctx.Enabled = true) and disable it on close, which hands those keys back to movement or camera. Default player scripts use IAS when Workspace.PlayerScriptsUseInputActionSystem is enabled.
B23: Roblox's UI Styling system is a CSS-like set of instances. StyleSheet holds the rules and tokens. StyleRule has a Selector (class name, .tag, #name, :state like :hover, descendant/child combinators) and property values set via SetProperty/SetProperties, plus a Priority. StyleDerive makes one sheet inherit rules from another (themes, base sheets). StyleLink is placed in a ScreenGui (or other UI root) and points at a StyleSheet, applying it to that UI tree. StyleQuery adds conditional rules (screen size, aspect ratio, input type). Styles reach the UI because a StyleLink connects the sheet to a UI tree, and its rules then match GuiObjects by class, tag (CollectionService or the styling tags) or name, the way CSS does. Rule priority and specificity resolve conflicts, and properties set directly on an instance override styles. Tokens: define attributes on a (token) StyleSheet, for example PrimaryColor = Color3, and reference them in rule values as "$PrimaryColor". Swapping or deriving token sheets changes the theme everywhere. The Studio Style Editor is still in beta, and the selector syntax may change.
B24: Roblox requires an age check to access chat, rolled out from late 2025 and globally in early 2026. It uses facial age estimation through the Roblox app, with a camera selfie processed by a vendor (Persona), and ID verification or parental controls can correct an estimate. Age groups: under 9, 9-12, 13-15, 16-17, 18-20 and 21+. Restriction: by default, users can chat only with their own age group and the adjacent groups (for example, 13-15 with 9-12 and 16-17), which keeps minors and adults apart (under-16s can't chat with adults). Under-9s need parental consent for chat. Trusted Connections (13+, verified real-world contacts) can chat beyond the bands. Unchecked users can't use chat. Messages from users you can't chat with are hidden from you.
